brief: LLM inference basics: prefill versus decode, time to first token, time per output token, throughput versus latency

outline.title: LLM inference fundamentals
outline.summary: You will be able to explain how an LLM turns a prompt into tokens, break a request's latency into prefill and decode, and reason about TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency and throughput when reading dashboards or choosing a deployment.
outline.prompt: I want to understand how LLM inference works end to end, including prefill versus decode and metrics like time to first token, time per output token and throughput, so that I can reason about latency and cost when building or operating LLM-powered features.

modules.title: How a request becomes tokens
modules.objective: Trace an LLM request from text through tokenization, the forward pass and the autoregressive loop back to streamed text.

bank.prompt: Your app sends the same customer-support reply in English and in Thai. The Thai version uses noticeably more tokens even though the meaning is the same. What is the most likely reason?
bank.reference: Subword tokenizers learn their vocabulary from training data, so text that was common in that data packs into fewer, longer tokens, and other scripts fragment into more pieces. The tempting mistake is assuming a fixed rule like one token per word or one per character, when the count really depends on the learned vocabulary.
options: The tokenizer's vocabulary covers frequent English pieces well, so less common scripts split into more, smaller tokens
Tokens are counted per character for non-Latin scripts, while English tokens are counted per whole word
The model inserts hidden translation tokens internally whenever it detects a non-English prompt
Thai text needs more bytes on the wire, and the API bills by request bytes rather than by tokens

bank.prompt: After the forward pass over your prompt, what does the model produce at the final position that is used to choose the next token?
bank.reference: The output is a logits vector with one score for every token in the vocabulary. Softmax and a decoding rule such as greedy or sampling then pick one token. A common misconception is that the model outputs a token directly, but the choice happens in a separate selection step.
options: A single token ID that the model has already committed to
A vector of scores, one per vocabulary entry, that a sampler turns into a choice
A probability for each word that appears in the prompt so far
An embedding of the whole response that is decoded in one step

bank.prompt: The diagram shows the generation loop. A request has a 1,000-token prompt and produces a 200-token answer. Assuming the engine caches earlier work with a KV cache, roughly how many forward passes does the whole request take?
bank.reference: The prompt is processed in one parallel pass, which yields the first output token, and each later token needs its own pass because it depends on the tokens before it, giving about 200 passes in total. Counting a pass per prompt token ignores that prompt tokens are processed together, and the loop runs per token, not per word.
options: A single pass that emits all 200 output tokens at once
About 1,200 passes, one for every prompt token and every output token
One pass over the whole prompt, then roughly one more pass per additional output token
One pass per output word, so fewer than 200 because words span several tokens

bank.prompt: Users report that long summaries end mid-sentence. For these cases the API response shows a finish reason of length rather than stop. Explain what happened and suggest one reasonable fix.
bank.reference: Generation was cut off because it hit the maximum output token limit (or the context limit) before the model emitted its end-of-sequence token or a stop sequence, so the model did not choose to stop. Fixes include raising max tokens, asking for shorter output, or detecting the length finish reason and handling or continuing the response.

bank.prompt: The diagram shows when text reaches the user with and without streaming. Your PM expects that turning on streaming will cut GPU cost and total completion time. What does streaming actually change?
bank.reference: Streaming sends each token or small chunk as soon as it is generated, so users see text much earlier, but the model still runs the same loop for the same number of tokens. The common mistake is believing streaming speeds up generation or lowers cost, when it only changes when the output is delivered.
options: Total completion time drops sharply because the model generates tokens faster when streaming
The output token count falls, because streamed chunks are billed as partial tokens
GPU cost per request falls, because the server can release the model once streaming starts
The time until the first text appears, while total generation time and token count stay about the same

bank.prompt: You raise the sampling temperature from 0.2 to 1.2 for a brainstorming feature. What changes in how the next token is selected?
bank.reference: Temperature rescales the logits as \( p_i \propto e^{z_i / T} \), so a larger T flattens the distribution and a smaller T sharpens it, while the forward pass itself is unchanged. The tempting wrong answer reverses the direction; multiplying by a larger T would make outputs more deterministic, not more varied.
options: Logits are divided by the temperature before softmax, flattening the distribution so less likely tokens are picked more often
The forward pass runs extra layers at higher temperature, producing more varied logits for the sampler
The vocabulary is expanded to include rarer tokens that are normally excluded from sampling
Logits are multiplied by the temperature before softmax, sharpening the distribution toward the top token

bank.prompt: A user types a question and presses send, with streaming on. Walk through, in order, what happens between the text arriving at the server and the first word appearing on their screen.
bank.reference: The text (usually wrapped in a chat template) is tokenized into token IDs; a forward pass runs over all prompt tokens and produces logits at the last position; a decoding step picks a token from those logits; that token is detokenized to text and sent as the first streamed chunk. The answer should note that the token is then appended and the loop repeats for later tokens.

bank.prompt: You expect 1 million requests a month, each with about 1,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens. Input costs 1 dollar per million tokens and output costs 4 dollars per million tokens. Using \( C = N(t_{in}p_{in} + t_{out}p_{out}) \), roughly what is the monthly bill?
bank.reference: Input is 1 billion tokens at 1 dollar per million, which is 1,000 dollars, and output is 200 million tokens at 4 dollars per million, which is 800 dollars, for about 1,800 dollars. The common mistakes are pricing all tokens at the input rate or ignoring output tokens, even though output is often priced higher per token.
options: About 1,200 dollars
About 1,800 dollars
About 4,800 dollars
About 1,000 dollars

bank.prompt: Your model confidently miscounts how many times the letter R appears in product codes like XRR-RRB-ARR. Using what you know about tokenization, explain why this kind of task is hard for the model and one way to make it easier.
bank.reference: The model sees token IDs, which often cover several characters with arbitrary boundaries, not individual letters, so it must infer spelling indirectly rather than reading characters. Making it easier means forcing character-level tokens, such as separating letters with spaces, or doing the counting in ordinary code instead of the model.

bank.prompt: The diagram shows a forward pass over the prompt 'The cat sat on'. The model computes a logits vector at every position. Which one determines the next token to be generated, and why?
bank.reference: With causal attention each position predicts the token after it, and only the last position has seen the entire prompt, so its logits pick the next token. The other positions' predictions are used in training, but they predict tokens that already exist in the prompt, so they do not yield multiple new tokens at once.
options: The average of all four logits vectors, so every prompt token contributes equally to the choice
Only the last position's logits, because it has attended to the whole prompt and predicts what follows it
The first position's logits, because attention summarizes the whole sequence into the first token
Each position's logits, so four new tokens are generated in parallel from one pass

bank.prompt: Your product must never emit one particular token, not even rarely. Which intervention in the decoding step guarantees that?
bank.reference: Masking the logit to negative infinity gives the token zero probability after softmax, so no decoding rule can select it. Lowering temperature or using top-p only reshapes probabilities, and if the banned token happens to score highest it can still be chosen, while prompt instructions are not guarantees.
options: Lower the temperature so the banned token becomes too unlikely to ever be sampled
Add a system prompt instruction telling the model never to produce that token
Set that token's logit to negative infinity before softmax so its probability becomes zero
Use top-p sampling with a small p so only high-probability tokens remain eligible

bank.prompt: In a load test, doubling the prompt from 500 to 1,000 tokens barely changes total latency, but doubling the output from 200 to 400 tokens nearly doubles it. What best explains this?
bank.reference: The whole prompt can be processed in one parallel forward pass, but each output token depends on the previous one, so output tokens require sequential passes and latency grows with output length. Engines do batch decode steps across users, so the batching explanation misreads where the sequential cost comes from.
options: Prompt tokens are processed together in parallel, while output tokens are produced one at a time, each needing its own pass
Output tokens are larger than prompt tokens, so each one takes more memory and compute to store
The tokenizer encodes output text more slowly than prompt text, adding time per output token
The server batches prompt tokens with other users' requests but never batches output tokens

bank.prompt: With greedy decoding, a model sometimes gets stuck repeating the same phrase until it hits the max tokens limit. Explain how the generation loop makes this self-reinforcing, and name one mitigation.
bank.reference: Each generated token is appended to the context, so once a phrase repeats, the repeated context makes the same continuation score highest again, and greedy always picks the top token so it never escapes. Mitigations include repetition or frequency penalties, sampling with some temperature, stop sequences, or a lower max tokens limit to cap the damage.

bank.prompt: You set a stop sequence of two newlines so the model returns exactly one paragraph. Some responses come back empty with a finish reason of stop. What is the most likely cause?
bank.reference: Stop sequences are checked against the generated output, so if the model opens with two newlines, generation stops immediately with nothing useful. Running out of max tokens would report a length finish reason, not stop, and stop sequences are normally matched in the output rather than the prompt.
options: The max tokens limit was too low, so the model ran out of budget before writing anything
The model began its output with a blank line pair, so the stop sequence matched before any content
The stop sequence also appears in the prompt, which ends generation before decoding begins
Two newlines tokenize to the end-of-sequence token, so the model halts on its first line break

bank.prompt: To cut costs, you lower max tokens to 150 on an endpoint that returns JSON. Typical responses are about 120 tokens, but some are 300. What is the main risk?
bank.reference: Max tokens is a hard cutoff applied by the engine, so a response that would run to 300 tokens simply stops at 150, typically leaving broken JSON. The tempting misconception is that the model knows the limit and plans a shorter answer, but unless it is told in the prompt, it generates as usual until it is truncated.
options: The model automatically shortens long answers to fit, so some fields quietly lose detail
Requests that would need longer answers are rejected before generation even starts
Long responses get cut off mid-object, producing invalid JSON that your parser rejects
Every response is padded out to 150 tokens, raising the cost of the short ones

bank.prompt: Your streaming client decodes and displays each token's bytes as soon as they arrive. Emoji and some accented characters sometimes appear as garbled symbols mid-stream, yet the final full text is correct. Diagnose the cause and suggest a fix.
bank.reference: A single character can be encoded as several bytes that are split across more than one token, so decoding each chunk on its own produces invalid partial characters. The fix is an incremental decoder that buffers incomplete byte sequences until the character is complete before displaying it.

modules.title: Prefill versus decode
modules.objective: Distinguish the prefill phase that processes the whole prompt in parallel from the decode phase that generates one token per step.
concepts: why decode is dominated by weight reads
how prompt and output length shift the balance

bank.prompt: The diagram shows the GPU timeline for one request with a 1,200-token prompt: one wide block, followed by a series of short, equal blocks. What happens during the wide first block?
bank.reference: Prefill runs every prompt position through the model at once, which is possible because all prompt tokens are already known. It writes keys and values into the KV cache and yields logits for the first output token. The tempting mistake is picturing prefill as a token-by-token loop like decode, which is exactly what the parallel pass avoids.
options: All 1,200 prompt tokens go through the model in one parallel forward pass, filling the KV cache and producing the first output token
The 1,200 prompt tokens go through the model one at a time, each step reading the weights again, before any output is produced
Only the last prompt token goes through the model, because earlier tokens are summarized by the tokenizer
The model weights are copied from disk into GPU memory for this request, and no tokens are processed yet

bank.prompt: Prefill handled a 2,000-token prompt in a single pass. A teammate asks why the engine cannot also produce all 200 output tokens in one pass. What is the real reason?
bank.reference: Decode is sequential because token n+1 depends on which token was actually sampled at step n, and that is unknown until the previous step finishes. The causal mask is a tempting answer, but prefill uses the same mask and still runs in parallel because its inputs are all known in advance.
options: Each output token is fed back as input for the next step, so it must be sampled before the next step can start
The causal attention mask forbids a token from attending to later positions, so outputs cannot be computed together
GPU memory cannot hold activations for 200 new positions at once, so they are split into single steps
The KV cache can only be appended once per forward pass, so it limits generation to one token per pass

bank.prompt: Profiling a 4,000-token prefill shows the GPU's matrix units near full utilization while memory bandwidth has headroom. What best explains why prefill is limited by compute?
bank.reference: In prefill the weights are loaded once and reused across every prompt position in a matrix-matrix multiply, so arithmetic per byte is high and compute becomes the bottleneck. Thinking that weights are re-read per prompt token describes a naive token loop, not a real prefill, and would make it memory-bound instead.
options: Each weight read from memory is multiplied against thousands of token vectors, so many operations are done per byte loaded
Prefill reads the full set of weights once per prompt token, which saturates the arithmetic units with load instructions
Building the KV cache needs more arithmetic than the matrix multiplications in the attention and MLP layers
Prefill runs the model at a higher numerical precision than decode, so each operation costs more compute

bank.concept: why decode is dominated by weight reads
bank.prompt: During decode at batch size 1, your GPU monitor shows memory bandwidth near its peak while arithmetic units sit mostly idle. Explain why decode behaves this way.
bank.reference: Each decode step processes only one new token but must still stream essentially all model weights (plus the KV cache) from GPU memory. With one token, every weight is used for only about two operations, so the step time is set by how fast bytes can be read, not by compute. Key points: one token per step, all weights read every step, low arithmetic per byte.

bank.concept: how prompt and output length shift the balance
bank.prompt: Same model, same idle GPU. Request A summarizes an 8,000-token document into 100 tokens. Request B writes a 1,500-token story from a 50-token prompt. What should you expect?
bank.reference: Prompt length drives prefill and therefore time to first token, while output length drives the number of sequential decode steps, so the long story's latency is mostly decode. The cache intuition is backwards: a longer context means a larger KV cache to read each step, so A's per-token speed is, if anything, slightly slower.
options: A has a much longer time to first token, while B spends most of its total time in decode
Both are dominated by prefill, since prefill is the compute-heavy phase of every request
B has the longer time to first token, because the model must plan all 1,500 tokens up front
A streams its output tokens faster than B, because its long prompt is already stored in cache

bank.prompt: You measure decode at about 20 ms per token. A colleague predicts a 1,000-token prompt will take about 20 seconds before the first token appears, since that is 1,000 times 20 ms. Explain why this prediction is badly wrong.
bank.reference: Prefill does not process prompt tokens one step at a time; it runs all of them through the model in one parallel pass. The weights are read once and reused for every prompt token, so the cost per prompt token is far lower than a decode step, which pays a full weight read for a single token. A good answer mentions the single parallel pass and the shared weight reads.

bank.concept: why decode is dominated by weight reads
bank.prompt: Decode benchmark on one GPU: batch 1 gives 50 tokens/s; batch 8 gives about 380 tokens/s in total, and each step takes only slightly longer. What best explains this?
bank.reference: At small batch sizes decode time is dominated by streaming the weights, and one read serves every sequence in the batch, so throughput rises almost linearly until compute becomes the limit. The overlap explanation fails because bandwidth was already near peak at batch 1; the gain comes from not reading the weights more times, not from reading them faster.
options: Each step reads the weights once and applies them to all 8 sequences, so the dominant cost is shared
Batching lets each sequence generate several future tokens in one step, multiplying the output rate
Batching splits the KV cache across sequences, so each step reads far less memory than at batch 1
The 8 separate weight reads overlap with each other, so the memory bus is used 8 times more efficiently

bank.prompt: A homegrown server feeds prompt tokens through the same one-token-per-step loop it uses for generation, using a KV cache throughout. With 2,000-token prompts, its time to first token is far worse than a mainstream engine on the same GPU. What is the main cause?
bank.reference: The total arithmetic is about the same either way; what changes is that a token loop reloads all weights for each prompt token instead of reusing one load across the whole prompt. The extra-FLOPs explanation is the tempting misconception: the slowdown comes from repeated memory traffic, not from more math.
options: Every prompt token pays a full read of the weights, so time to first token scales with prompt length times a decode step
Processing tokens one at a time performs many more total arithmetic operations than a single parallel pass would
Without one parallel pass the KV cache cannot be stored, so attention over the prompt is recomputed at every token
The loop samples a token after every prompt position, and that sampling work dominates the time to first token

bank.prompt: With the same prompt and an otherwise idle server, a 500-token answer takes noticeably longer to finish than a 100-token answer, even though both started streaming at the same moment. Predict roughly how the time after the first token compares, and explain why.
bank.reference: Time after the first token grows roughly in proportion to the number of output tokens, so the 500-token answer takes about five times as long after the first token. Decode produces one token per forward pass and each step must wait for the previous token, so steps cannot be overlapped for a single sequence.

bank.prompt: Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose several tokens, which the large model then checks in a single forward pass. Why can this cut latency for a single request?
bank.reference: Decode is slow because each step reads all weights for one token; verifying k proposed tokens in one pass processes them in parallel, like prefill, so accepted tokens share one weight read. The output still matches what the large model would accept, so it is not simply the draft model's output being passed through.
options: Checking several proposed tokens at once works like a small prefill, so one read of the large model's weights covers several positions
The large model skips most of its layers for proposed tokens, so each verification step does much less work
Proposed tokens are emitted without involving the large model, so most output comes from the cheaper model alone
Verifying proposals shrinks the KV cache the large model must read, so every step needs less memory traffic

bank.prompt: Estimate the prefill time for a 4,000-token prompt on an 8B-parameter model, using \( \text{FLOPs} \approx 2 \times N_{\text{params}} \times T_{\text{prompt}} \), on a GPU that sustains 400 TFLOP/s for this work. Ignore attention cost and overheads.
bank.reference: Two times 8e9 times 4,000 is 6.4e13 FLOPs, and dividing by 4e14 FLOP/s gives about 0.16 s. The most common slip is dropping the factor of two (one multiply and one add per weight per token), which gives 80 ms.
options: About 160 ms
About 80 ms
About 16 ms
About 1.6 s

bank.prompt: The diagram is a roofline: achieved FLOP/s against arithmetic intensity. Say where a 2,000-token prefill and a batch-1 decode step fall, and predict which one speeds up on a GPU with twice the FLOP/s but the same memory bandwidth.
bank.reference: The 2,000-token prefill has high arithmetic intensity because weights are reused across all prompt tokens, so it sits on the flat compute ceiling and benefits from more FLOP/s. Batch-1 decode does little arithmetic per byte read, so it sits on the bandwidth slope and barely changes when only compute is doubled.

bank.concept: why decode is dominated by weight reads
bank.prompt: A 13B-parameter model is served with 16-bit weights on a GPU with about 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. Using \( t_{\text{step}} \gtrsim \frac{\text{weight bytes}}{\text{bandwidth}} \), what is the approximate lower bound on decode step time at batch size 1?
bank.reference: 13B parameters at 2 bytes each is about 26 GB, and 26 GB divided by 2 TB/s is about 13 ms per step, capping a single stream near 75 tokens/s. The 6.5 ms answer comes from counting one byte per parameter, which forgets that 16-bit weights take two bytes each.
options: About 13 ms
About 6.5 ms
About 1.3 ms
About 130 ms

bank.concept: why decode is dominated by weight reads
bank.prompt: You switch a model from 16-bit weights to 4-bit weight-only quantization, keeping activations in 16-bit. For low-concurrency traffic, what change in prefill and decode speed is most likely?
bank.reference: Small-batch decode is bound by streaming weights, so cutting weight bytes by about four times directly shortens each step, though not fully fourfold because of the KV cache and overheads. Prefill is compute-bound and weight-only quantization does not reduce its matrix arithmetic, so its gain is small. The no-speedup answer wrongly assumes decode is limited by arithmetic.
options: Decode gets substantially faster because each step reads far fewer weight bytes, while prefill gains much less
Prefill gets about four times faster because weights are smaller, while decode is unchanged because of KV cache reads
Both phases get about four times faster, since every phase scales with the size of the weights
Neither phase gets faster, because the number of arithmetic operations per token stays the same

bank.concept: how prompt and output length shift the balance
bank.prompt: Your feature moves from chat (short prompts, long answers) to retrieval-augmented answers with about 6,000 tokens of context and about 150-token answers. Predict how time to first token and per-token streaming speed change, and which phase now deserves more optimization attention.
bank.reference: Time to first token rises sharply because prefill now processes thousands of tokens, so prefill becomes a much larger share of latency and GPU compute. Per-token streaming gets only somewhat slower, because each decode step also reads a larger KV cache. Prefill, and techniques that cut its cost such as reusing shared prompt prefixes, deserves more attention than before.

bank.concept: how prompt and output length shift the balance
bank.prompt: The plot shows decode step time for one long generation at batch 1. Step time climbs gradually and steadily as the sequence grows. What is the most likely cause?
bank.reference: Beyond the fixed weight reads, each decode step reads keys and values for every earlier token, so per-step cost rises gently and roughly linearly with context length. Re-running prefill each step would happen without a KV cache and would make step time grow far faster, not a modest drift on top of a large fixed cost.
options: Each step also reads the KV cache, which grows with every token, so memory traffic per step slowly increases
The engine is re-running prefill over the whole sequence each step, so step cost grows with sequence length
The GPU is thermally throttling over time, so every operation gets steadily slower as the run continues
Sampling the next token costs more as the output grows, because more candidate tokens must be compared

modules.title: Latency metrics that users feel
modules.objective: Define and calculate TTFT, TPOT, inter-token latency and end-to-end latency for a single request.

bank.prompt: A user hits send in a chat app that streams its replies. Which interval does time to first token (TTFT) measure for that request?
bank.reference: TTFT is the wait the user feels before anything appears, so it covers everything before the first token: network, queueing, tokenization and prefill. The most tempting mistake is to count only prefill, which hides queueing delay, often the largest part under load.
options: From the request being sent until the first output token reaches the user, including any queueing and prefill.
From the start of prefill until the first output token is produced, excluding any time spent waiting in a queue.
From the first output token until the last output token, divided by the number of output tokens generated.
From the request being sent until the full response has been received and rendered by the client.

bank.prompt: A request produces 201 output tokens. Its TTFT is 0.2 s and its end-to-end latency is 4.2 s. What is the time per output token (TPOT) for this request?
bank.reference: TPOT covers only the decode phase after the first token: \( \text{TPOT} = \frac{E2E - TTFT}{N - 1} = \frac{4.0\text{ s}}{200} = 20\text{ ms} \). Common errors are dividing the whole E2E by all 201 tokens, which mixes prefill and queueing into the per-token figure, or dividing by 201 instead of the 200 gaps after the first token.
options: 20 ms
About 20.9 ms
About 19.9 ms
21 ms

bank.prompt: The diagram shows when each of eight streamed tokens arrived for one response, with the gaps between them labelled in milliseconds. Which statement best describes this request?
bank.reference: TPOT averages the decode time over the gaps: (6 × 25 + 300) / 7 ≈ 64 ms. Inter-token latency is the distribution of individual gaps, so its maximum or tail exposes the 300 ms stall. Believing TPOT discards outliers leads teams to miss stutters users clearly notice.
options: Mean TPOT is about 64 ms, but a maximum inter-token latency of 300 ms reveals a visible stall the average hides.
TPOT is 25 ms, because the single long gap is an outlier and TPOT excludes outliers by definition.
TPOT and inter-token latency are both 300 ms, because the slowest gap sets the generation rate.
Inter-token latency is about 64 ms and TPOT is 300 ms, because TPOT reports the worst gap.

bank.prompt: Under current load your model has a TTFT of 500 ms and a TPOT of 30 ms. A user asks for an answer that will be 301 tokens long. What end-to-end latency should you estimate?
bank.reference: \( E2E = TTFT + TPOT \times (N - 1) = 0.5 + 0.03 \times 300 = 9.5\text{ s} \). The first token is already covered by TTFT, so only the remaining 300 tokens add TPOT; the most common slip is ignoring TTFT entirely, which gives 9.0 s.
options: About 9.53 s
About 9.03 s

bank.prompt: During peak hours your p99 TTFT doubles. Prompt lengths are unchanged, and server logs show the prefill step itself takes the same time as off-peak. Explain where the extra TTFT is most likely coming from.
bank.reference: TTFT includes time a request spends waiting before its prefill starts. At peak, requests queue for a free batch slot or memory, so the wait grows while prefill duration stays flat. A good answer names queueing or scheduling wait as part of TTFT, not slower prefill.

bank.prompt: You run two features on the same model: a streaming chat assistant and a backend job that returns a complete JSON summary in one response. For each, which latency the user actually waits on matters most, and why?
bank.reference: For streaming chat, users feel TTFT first and then TPOT as reading speed, so the full E2E matters less once text is flowing. For the non-streaming JSON job, nothing is usable until the last token, so the user waits the whole E2E, which is TTFT plus TPOT times the remaining output tokens and is dominated by output length for long responses.

bank.prompt: On an otherwise idle server, you grow a request's prompt from 500 tokens to 8,000 tokens while keeping output length the same. What change in latency should you expect?
bank.reference: Prefill processes the whole prompt before the first token, so its cost and therefore TTFT grows with prompt length. Each decode step only adds one token while reading a longer KV cache, so TPOT grows only modestly. The tempting error is thinking parallel prefill is free; it is parallel, but the total work still scales with prompt tokens.
options: TTFT rises substantially because prefill must process every prompt token, while TPOT rises only modestly.
TTFT and TPOT both rise roughly sixteen-fold, because every phase scales with prompt length equally.
TTFT stays roughly flat because prefill runs in parallel, while TPOT rises sharply with prompt size.
TPOT rises a lot because each new token rereads the prompt, while TTFT is essentially unchanged.

bank.prompt: Your client SDK records a p50 TTFT of 900 ms, but the inference server's own metrics report a p50 TTFT of 300 ms for the same traffic. Diagnose the likely causes of the gap.
bank.reference: The server usually starts its clock when the engine receives or admits the request, while the client measures from send to first token on screen. The difference comes from things outside the server's view: network round trips and connection setup, gateways, auth or rate-limit layers, queueing in a proxy or load balancer, and any buffering of the streamed response. The user-felt TTFT is the client number.

bank.prompt: A dashboard reports a TPOT of 25 ms for a replica serving many concurrent users. A colleague concludes the replica generates 40 tokens per second in total. What is the correct interpretation?
bank.reference: TPOT is a per-request decode metric: 25 ms per token means about 40 tokens per second for that one stream. Because many requests decode together in a batch, aggregate throughput is roughly per-stream rate times the number of concurrent decoding requests. Confusing per-request speed with system throughput is a common mistake.
options: Each request streams at about 40 tokens per second; total replica throughput is roughly that rate times concurrent streams.
The replica produces 40 tokens per second in total, split evenly among however many users are currently connected.
Each request streams at 25 tokens per second, since TPOT in milliseconds equals the per-user token rate.
Total throughput is 40 tokens per second divided by the batch size, since batching slows each request.

bank.prompt: A classification endpoint returns 5 output tokens. Client logs show a TTFT of 2.0 s and an end-to-end latency of 2.2 s. A dashboard computes per-token time as end-to-end latency divided by output tokens. What is this request's actual TPOT?
bank.reference: Only the 0.2 s after the first token is decode time, spread over 4 gaps: \( \frac{2.2 - 2.0}{5 - 1} = 50\text{ ms} \). Dividing E2E by output tokens gives 440 ms, folding queueing and prefill into the per-token number, which badly distorts short responses.
options: 50 ms
40 ms
440 ms
400 ms

bank.prompt: Two deployments both report a TPOT of 30 ms and identical end-to-end latency for a 300-token answer. In one, tokens arrive about every 30 ms. In the other, a proxy buffers output so tokens arrive in bursts of five roughly every 150 ms. Which statement is accurate?
bank.reference: Equal TPOT and E2E mean the same average gap, but inter-token latency describes each individual gap, and buffering creates a bimodal pattern of near-zero and 150 ms gaps. The tempting error is assuming the same TPOT implies the same streaming experience.
options: The buffered one has mostly near-zero gaps plus a 150 ms gap every fifth token, so it looks choppier despite equal TPOT.
The buffered one effectively has a 150 ms TPOT, so its end-to-end latency must be about five times higher.
The buffered one has lower inter-token latency on average, so users will perceive its text as smoother.
Both have identical inter-token latency distributions, because the distribution is determined by TPOT.

bank.prompt: You are choosing between two configurations. One has TTFT 0.3 s and TPOT 40 ms; the other has TTFT 1.5 s and TPOT 20 ms. Your product has short replies of about 20 tokens and long reports of about 500 tokens. Which statement about end-to-end latency is correct?
bank.reference: For 20 tokens: 0.3 + 19 × 0.04 ≈ 1.06 s versus 1.5 + 19 × 0.02 ≈ 1.88 s. For 500 tokens: 0.3 + 499 × 0.04 ≈ 20.3 s versus 1.5 + 499 × 0.02 ≈ 11.5 s. Which metric dominates depends on output length, so neither is always the bottleneck.
options: The low-TTFT configuration is faster for short replies, while the low-TPOT one is faster for long reports.
The low-TPOT configuration is faster for both, because decode time always dominates end-to-end latency.
The low-TTFT configuration is faster for both, because the initial wait dominates end-to-end latency.
Both are about equal for long reports, because the TTFT difference cancels out the TPOT difference.

bank.prompt: An API gateway kills non-streaming requests after 10 s. Under normal load your model has a TTFT of about 0.4 s and a TPOT of about 50 ms, and max output tokens is set to 300. Predict whether long answers will be cut off, and say what you would change.
bank.reference: Yes: a 300-token answer takes roughly 0.4 s plus 299 × 50 ms, about 15 s, well past the 10 s limit; only around 190 tokens fit. Fixes include lowering max output tokens with margin for load, raising the timeout, or streaming the response. A good answer estimates E2E from TTFT plus TPOT times output tokens and notes that latency rises under heavier load.

bank.prompt: The plot shows p50 TTFT and measured prefill duration on one replica as request rate increases, with identical prompts throughout. What best explains the sharp rise in TTFT at higher request rates?
bank.reference: Prefill duration is flat in the plot, so the extra TTFT is waiting time before prefill, which grows non-linearly as utilization nears capacity. Blaming slower prefill contradicts the measured data, and TTFT ends at the first token, so it does not include full decode.
options: Requests wait longer before their prefill starts as arrivals approach the replica's capacity.
Each prefill takes longer at high load because the prompts end up being processed token by token.
TTFT includes decoding the full response, which lengthens when more users are active at once.
Network bandwidth between client and server saturates, slowing delivery of the prompt bytes.

bank.prompt: The diagram breaks down TTFT for a typical request on your service. You need to cut p50 TTFT by at least half. Which change most directly targets the component that makes this possible?
bank.reference: Queue wait is 800 ms of the 1.2 s, so halving TTFT requires shrinking the wait, which means more capacity or less admitted load. Prefix caching and shorter prompts only attack the 300 ms prefill, which cannot deliver a 600 ms saving, and speculative decoding affects TPOT, not TTFT.
options: Add serving capacity or limit admitted load so that requests begin prefill sooner.
Enable prefix caching so that repeated system prompt tokens can skip prefill.
Use speculative decoding to reduce the time spent per output token.
Shorten prompts by about 20 percent to reduce the amount of prefill work.

modules.title: Throughput and the latency trade-off
modules.objective: Explain throughput as tokens per second across all users and why raising it usually costs per-request latency.
concepts: per-request versus aggregate tokens per second
concurrency and its effect on tpot
requests per second versus tokens per second

bank.concept: per-request versus aggregate tokens per second
bank.prompt: Your serving dashboard shows 2,400 output tokens/s on one replica, yet each user sees text stream at only about 40 tokens/s. What best explains the gap?
bank.reference: Aggregate throughput sums the output of every concurrent stream, so 2,400 tokens/s spread over about 60 streams gives each user about 40 tokens/s. The tempting mistake is to read the aggregate number as the speed one user should see and blame the network for the difference.
options: The replica is decoding about 60 requests at once, and 2,400 is their combined rate
Network buffering holds back tokens, so users receive only part of the generation rate
Users perceive the slower first-token phase, while the dashboard shows steady decode
Each request generates 60 tokens per step, which are then trickled out to the client

bank.prompt: A vendor benchmark reports 25,000 tokens/s on a summarization test with 4,000-token inputs and 100-token outputs. Your chat app uses 300-token inputs and 400-token outputs. Why shouldn't you expect anything near 25,000 tokens/s?
bank.reference: Prefill handles all prompt tokens in one parallel pass, so input tokens are processed far faster per token than output tokens, which decode generates one step at a time. A combined tokens/s figure dominated by input tokens says little about an output-heavy workload, and believing output tokens are the cheap ones gets the cost asymmetry backwards.
options: The figure is mostly input tokens, which prefill processes in parallel far faster than decode emits outputs
Summarization uses smaller models, so the figure only applies to that class of model
Output tokens are cheaper than input tokens, so your chat app would exceed the figure
Long inputs warm the KV cache, which speeds up every later request in the benchmark

bank.concept: concurrency and its effect on tpot
bank.prompt: The chart shows aggregate output throughput on one replica at four concurrency levels. Compared with serving a single request, what happens to each user's time per output token at concurrency 64?
bank.reference: At concurrency 1, TPOT is 1/50 s, or 20 ms. At 64, each stream gets about 1,150/64, roughly 18 tokens/s, so TPOT is about 55 ms. Reading the aggregate rate as a per-user rate gives the 0.9 ms error, and assuming requests run one after another gives the 1.3 s error, but batched requests share each decode step.
options: It rises to roughly 55 ms, because each stream now gets about 18 tokens/s
It falls to about 0.9 ms, because the replica now emits 1,150 tokens/s
It stays near 20 ms, because total throughput kept growing with concurrency
It rises to about 1.3 s, because the 64 requests take turns on each decode step

bank.concept: requests per second versus tokens per second
bank.prompt: Your service comfortably handles 10 requests per second. A product change keeps request volume the same, but average responses grow from 200 to 1,000 output tokens. Predict what happens to the service, and explain why requests per second hid the risk.
bank.reference: Output token demand rises about fivefold, and each request holds a decode slot about five times longer, so concurrency climbs, TPOT worsens, and the replicas may saturate and start queueing, which raises TTFT. Requests per second is not a capacity measure on its own, because the load depends on how many tokens each request carries.

bank.prompt: To cut GPU cost, an operator raises the maximum number of concurrent sequences per replica until the GPUs run near full utilization at peak. Which outcome is most likely for interactive users during peak?
bank.reference: Packing more sequences into each decode step raises tokens per GPU-second, which lowers cost, but each step takes longer, so TPOT rises. Running near saturation also leaves no headroom for bursts, so queueing pushes up TTFT. The common mistake is to assume a busier GPU means each request also finishes faster.
options: Cost per token falls, but TPOT rises and requests wait longer in queue, raising TTFT
Cost and latency both fall, since busier GPUs finish each request sooner
Latency stays the same, since utilization affects only throughput, not request speed
TTFT and TPOT both improve, since more slots mean requests never have to wait

bank.concept: requests per second versus tokens per second
bank.prompt: Two services each receive 5 requests per second on identical hardware. Service X averages 500 input and 50 output tokens per request; service Y averages 500 input and 800 output tokens. Which statement is right?
bank.reference: Decode load scales with output tokens per second: 4,000 for Y versus 250 for X, a factor of 16, and each Y request also stays active far longer. Adding input and output tokens together as if they cost the same ignores that output tokens are much more expensive to generate than prompt tokens are to prefill.
options: Y needs far more decode capacity, since it generates 16 times as many output tokens/s
Both need the same capacity, since the request rate is what drives serving load
Y needs about 2.4 times X's capacity, since its requests total 1,300 tokens versus 550
X needs more capacity, since its short outputs mean more prefill work per output token

bank.prompt: You run one model for two jobs: an interactive chat assistant and a nightly batch that labels 2 million documents. Would you configure concurrency the same way for both? Explain the trade-off you are making.
bank.reference: No. For the batch job, push concurrency and batch size high to maximize aggregate throughput and minimize cost per token, since nobody waits on any single response. For chat, cap concurrency and keep headroom so TTFT and TPOT stay within user-facing targets, accepting lower utilization and a higher cost per token in exchange for responsiveness.

bank.concept: per-request versus aggregate tokens per second
bank.prompt: At concurrency 64, one replica delivers 1,920 aggregate output tokens/s, about 30 tokens/s per stream, which meets your target. You expect 256 concurrent streams at peak. What is the most reasonable replica estimate?
bank.reference: The tested operating point, 64 streams at about 30 tokens/s each, meets the target, so 256 streams need about 256/64 = 4 replicas. Packing all 256 streams onto one replica would not keep per-stream speed constant: aggregate throughput grows sublinearly, so each stream's TPOT would rise well past the target.
options: About 4 replicas, each carrying 64 streams at roughly 30 tokens/s
1 replica, since raising its concurrency to 256 keeps streams near 30 tokens/s
About 2 replicas, since aggregate throughput doubles each time concurrency doubles
About 16 replicas, so that every stream runs at single-request decode speed

bank.concept: per-request versus aggregate tokens per second
bank.prompt: A load test reports 4,000 output tokens/s per replica, and the team calls it fast. During the same test, a tester notices responses streaming noticeably slower than when they use the model alone. Explain how both observations can be true.
bank.reference: The 4,000 tokens/s is an aggregate across many concurrent streams. Each stream's rate is roughly that total divided by concurrency, and batching more requests makes every decode step slower, which raises each user's TPOT. High aggregate throughput and slower individual streams are therefore consistent, and per-request metrics should be reported alongside the aggregate.

bank.prompt: You size a RAG service with 6,000-token prompts and 150-token answers. You use a benchmark that reported only output tokens/s, measured with short chat prompts. Why might it overestimate how many RAG users one replica can serve?
bank.reference: With 6,000-token prompts, prefill becomes a large share of GPU work, and it also competes with decode steps for other users. A benchmark of output throughput on short prompts never measured that cost. Input tokens are cheaper per token than output tokens, but not free, and long prompts also make each decode step slower, because there is more context to attend to.
options: Prefilling long prompts takes substantial GPU time that an output-only, short-prompt figure never captured
The output figure ignores the 150-token answers, which are the expensive part of a RAG request
Long prompts make each output token cheaper, so the benchmark actually underestimates capacity
The benchmark is accurate, since an input token costs the same GPU time as an output token

bank.concept: concurrency and its effect on tpot
bank.prompt: The plot shows median TPOT as the decode batch grows on one GPU. Why does TPOT stay nearly flat up to about 32 sequences and then climb steeply?
bank.reference: At small batch sizes, each decode step is dominated by streaming the model weights from memory, and that cost is shared across every sequence in the batch, so adding sequences is nearly free. As the batch grows, per-sequence KV cache reads and compute add up and step time rises. The tempting error is to call small-batch decode compute bound, when it is memory-bandwidth bound.
options: Small-batch decode is limited by reading weights from memory each step, which the whole batch shares
Small batches are compute bound, and extra sequences cost time only once GPU memory is full
Per-step time is set by client network latency until the outbound bandwidth saturates
Up to 32 sequences fit in one group of GPU cores, and beyond that they run one after another

bank.concept: concurrency and its effect on tpot
bank.prompt: After you raise max concurrent sequences from 32 to 128, aggregate output throughput rises 60% and median TPOT goes from 25 ms to 45 ms. Your chat product targets p95 TPOT under 50 ms. Was this a good change? Justify your answer and say what you would check.
bank.reference: The change improves cost per token, and the median still meets the target, but a 45 ms median is close enough to 50 ms that p95 likely exceeds it. Check p95 and p99 TPOT, and TTFT, under real peak traffic. If the tail misses the target, choose an intermediate concurrency cap that trades some throughput for meeting the latency target.

bank.concept: requests per second versus tokens per second
bank.prompt: After a prompt-template change, the maximum request rate your service can sustain within its latency SLO fell from 12 to 7 requests per second. Peak tokens/s per replica stayed about the same. What is the most likely explanation?
bank.reference: If token throughput is unchanged but sustainable requests per second dropped, each request must consume more tokens, for example a longer template or longer outputs. Broken batching or slower GPUs would show up as a drop in tokens/s, which did not happen.
options: Each request now carries more tokens, so the same token capacity serves fewer requests
The GPUs got slower, and flat tokens/s is masking a hidden hardware regression
The template broke batching, so the replica now serves requests one at a time
Users send fewer requests, so the measured rate is now limited by demand instead

bank.concept: requests per second versus tokens per second
bank.prompt: Your feature will see 20 requests per second, each generating 500 output tokens, and each stream decodes at about 25 tokens/s. Using \(L = \lambda W\), roughly how many requests are decoding at once on average?
bank.reference: Each request decodes for about 500/25 = 20 s, so \(L = 20 \times 20 = 400\) concurrent streams, ignoring TTFT. Equating concurrency with the arrival rate forgets that every request stays active for its whole generation time, which is why long outputs inflate concurrency and TPOT.
options: About 400, since each request spends about 20 seconds decoding
About 20, since average concurrency equals the arrival rate
About 10,000, since that is the output tokens/s the feature needs
About 0.8, since 20 requests are divided by 25 tokens/s per stream

bank.prompt: The plot shows p99 TTFT against offered load for one replica, with your SLO marked. A capacity planner proposes running replicas at 95% of max throughput to cut cost. What is the best response?
bank.reference: Queueing delay grows non-linearly as load approaches capacity, so p99 TTFT is modest up to around 75 to 85% load but far exceeds the 2 s SLO at 95%. The right operating point keeps headroom below where the curve crosses the SLO. Assuming that utilization affects only throughput ignores queueing, while capping at 60% gives up capacity the plot shows is safe.
options: Target well below 95% load, since p99 TTFT climbs steeply near saturation and 95% breaks the SLO
Accept 95% load, since higher utilization raises throughput without affecting tail latency
Target 60% load at most, since any load above that level already breaks the latency SLO
Accept 95% load but cap batch size, since TTFT depends only on batch size, not on load

bank.prompt: Average GPU utilization over the day is only 40%, yet users report p99 TTFT spikes of several seconds around 9 a.m. Diagnose what is happening and suggest one fix.
bank.reference: The daily average hides a burst: at the morning peak, arrivals briefly exceed capacity, so requests queue and TTFT spikes, while quiet hours pull the average down. This is a lack of headroom at peak, not a utilization problem. Fixes include scaling out replicas ahead of the peak, adding admission control or prioritization, or reserving capacity sized for peak load rather than the average.

modules.title: What drives inference speed
modules.objective: Identify the main levers, such as model size, prompt length, output length and hardware, that change TTFT and TPOT.

bank.prompt: You replace a 70B-parameter model with an 8B-parameter model on the same GPU, at the same 16-bit precision, serving one request at a time. What do you expect to happen to time per output token (TPOT)?
bank.reference: Each decode step at batch size 1 has to stream essentially all model weights from GPU memory, so per-token time scales roughly with the bytes of weights. An 8B model has about a ninth of the weight bytes of a 70B model. The tempting mistake is thinking model size only matters for prefill, when decode is the phase most directly tied to weight size.
options: It drops substantially, roughly in line with the smaller amount of weight data read per token
It stays about the same, because TPOT is set mainly by how many tokens are generated
Only TTFT improves, because model size affects prefill but not the decode steps
It drops only slightly, because attention over the context dominates each decode step

bank.prompt: On an idle server, a single request's prompt grows from 1,000 to 8,000 tokens while the output length stays the same. What happens to time to first token (TTFT)?
bank.reference: Prefill does work for every prompt token, so at these lengths TTFT grows roughly linearly with prompt length; attention adds a quadratic term that only becomes significant at long contexts. The common misconception is that parallel processing makes prefill free: parallelism makes it efficient, but the total compute still scales with the number of tokens.
options: It grows roughly in proportion to prompt length, since prefill must process every prompt token
It stays roughly constant, since all prompt tokens are processed in parallel during prefill
It grows with the square of prompt length right from the shortest prompts upward
It stays constant, since TTFT depends mainly on how many output tokens are requested

bank.prompt: A feature changes from generating 50-token summaries to 800-token reports, with the same prompt and model. Predict how TTFT and total response time change, and explain why.
bank.reference: TTFT stays roughly the same, because it depends on prefilling the unchanged prompt. Total time grows roughly linearly with the number of output tokens, because each extra token costs about one TPOT, so total is about \( \text{TTFT} + (N-1)\cdot\text{TPOT} \) and the report takes many times longer to finish.

bank.prompt: At batch size 1, profiling shows prefill keeps the GPU's math units busy, while decode leaves them mostly idle and saturates memory bandwidth. What best explains the difference?
bank.reference: In prefill, each weight read is reused across many prompt tokens, giving high arithmetic intensity, so it is compute bound. In decode, one token per step means all the weights are read to do only a small amount of math, so memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. The tempting error is assuming decode is slow because it does more math, when it actually does less math per byte moved.
options: Decode produces one token per step, so each full read of the weights feeds very little arithmetic
Decode needs more floating point operations per token than prefill, which overwhelms memory
Prefill reads the KV cache from host memory, while decode keeps it entirely in GPU registers
Decode is limited by CPU-side tokenization of each new token, which leaves the GPU waiting

bank.prompt: Every request to your assistant starts with the same 4,000-token system prompt followed by a short user message. You enable prefix caching on the inference server. What change should you expect?
bank.reference: Prefix caching reuses the stored KV cache for the shared leading tokens, so prefill only has to process the new suffix, which cuts TTFT. Decode still attends over the full context and reads the same weights, so TPOT is essentially unchanged. The common misconception is confusing prefix caching with whole-response caching, which requires an identical full prompt.
options: TTFT falls because only the new user tokens need prefill, while TPOT stays about the same
TPOT falls sharply because the cached prefix makes the KV cache smaller during decode
Neither metric changes, because caching only helps when the entire prompt is an exact repeat
TTFT rises slightly because cache lookups cost more than recomputing the system prompt

bank.prompt: An 8B model in 16-bit weights (about 16 GB) runs on a GPU with roughly 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. A teammate claims 2 ms per output token at batch size 1, without quantization or speculative decoding. Explain why you are skeptical.
bank.reference: At batch size 1 each decode step must read essentially all 16 GB of weights, so per-token time is bounded by \( t \geq \frac{\text{weight bytes}}{\text{bandwidth}} \), about 8 ms here. Claiming 2 ms would need about four times the bandwidth or a quarter of the bytes, for example via quantization, or a technique like speculative decoding that produces several tokens per weight read.

bank.prompt: Both requests run on the same server with a TPOT of 20 ms. Request A has a 200-token prompt, a TTFT of 0.1 s and 1,000 output tokens. Request B has a 4,000-token prompt, a TTFT of 0.4 s and 100 output tokens. Which finishes first?
bank.reference: Total time is about \( \text{TTFT} + (N-1)\cdot\text{TPOT} \): A is about 0.1 + 999 x 0.02, roughly 20 s, and B is about 0.4 + 99 x 0.02, roughly 2.4 s. The tempting mistake is judging speed by TTFT alone, when for long outputs the decode phase dominates total latency.
options: B finishes first, at about 2.4 s, while A takes about 20 s
A finishes first, because its TTFT is four times shorter than B's
They finish at about the same time, since B's longer prompt offsets its shorter output
B finishes first, but only by about 0.3 s, the gap between their TTFTs

bank.prompt: You benchmark a 7B and a 70B dense model on hardware with enough memory for both, using the same 2,000-token prompt at the same precision. Prefill is compute bound for both. Roughly how should their TTFT compare?
bank.reference: Forward-pass compute is roughly \( 2 \cdot P \cdot \text{tokens} \) FLOPs, so with ten times the parameters a compute-bound prefill takes roughly ten times as long. A common mistake is believing model size only matters for decode, but prefill compute grows directly with parameter count.
options: The 70B model's TTFT is roughly 10 times longer, since prefill compute scales with parameters times tokens
The TTFTs are about equal, since prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel for both models
The 70B model's TTFT is roughly 100 times longer, since compute grows with the square of parameter count
The TTFTs are about equal, since model size only affects the per-token decode speed

bank.prompt: A mixture-of-experts model has about 47B total parameters but uses only about 13B per token. At batch size 1, its TPOT is closer to that of a 13B dense model, yet it needs as much GPU memory as a 47B model. Explain both observations.
bank.reference: Each token is routed through only a few experts, so a decode step reads and computes with roughly the active parameters, which sets TPOT near that of a 13B dense model. All experts must still be stored in memory because different tokens may use any of them, so memory needs follow the total parameter count. A strong answer may add that at larger batches more experts are touched per step, which reduces this speed advantage.

bank.prompt: After a release of your retrieval-augmented assistant, median TTFT jumps from 300 ms to 1.5 s. TPOT, traffic and hardware are unchanged. What would you check first, and why?
bank.reference: Check whether prompts got longer, for example more or larger retrieved chunks, a longer system prompt or more conversation history being included. Prefill cost grows with prompt tokens, so a big TTFT increase with unchanged TPOT, traffic and hardware points to more input tokens rather than a slower decode path. A strong answer may also mention checking whether a prefix cache stopped hitting.

bank.prompt: A support bot has a 300-token prompt, a TTFT of 150 ms, a TPOT of 30 ms and answers averaging 600 tokens. Users complain that complete answers take too long. Which single change most reduces total response time?
bank.reference: Total time is about 0.15 + 599 x 0.03, roughly 18 s, almost all of it decode, so halving the output saves about 9 s. Trimming the prompt or caching it only shaves part of the 150 ms TTFT, and extra compute barely helps decode, which is memory bandwidth bound. The tempting mistake is optimizing TTFT when output length dominates total latency.
options: Prompt the model to answer concisely, cutting average output to about 300 tokens
Trim the system prompt so the total input shrinks from 300 to 150 tokens
Enable prefix caching so the shared system prompt is not prefilled again on each request
Move to a GPU with twice the compute FLOPs but the same memory bandwidth

bank.prompt: The diagram shows measured decode TPOT against batch size for one model on one GPU. TPOT stays almost flat from batch size 1 to about 16, then climbs. What best explains the flat region?
bank.reference: At small batches decode is memory bandwidth bound. The step time is mostly the cost of streaming the weights, which is paid once per step however many sequences share it, so extra sequences add little time. As the batch grows, the arithmetic and the per-sequence KV cache reads grow until compute or KV cache memory traffic becomes the limit, and TPOT rises. The tempting error is thinking batching reduces work per token, when it only reuses each weight read.
options: Each step is dominated by reading the weights once, and all sequences in the batch share that read
Batching lowers the floating point operations needed per token, offsetting the extra sequences
The GPU raises its clock speed under heavier load, hiding the extra work of larger batches
Larger batches shrink each sequence's KV cache, so less memory traffic is needed per step

bank.prompt: You are considering a new GPU with about twice the compute throughput of your current one but about the same memory bandwidth. For a chat service at small batch sizes, predict how TTFT and TPOT would change, and justify your prediction.
bank.reference: TTFT should improve, up to roughly twofold for longer prompts, because prefill is compute bound. TPOT should barely change, because small-batch decode is limited by how fast the weights can be read from memory, and the bandwidth stays the same.

bank.prompt: The diagram shows the token layout of two consecutive requests from your app. Prefix caching is enabled, but the cache hit rate is near zero and TTFT has not improved. What is the most likely cause?
bank.reference: Prefix caches reuse KV entries for an identical run of tokens starting at the beginning of the prompt, and since each token's KV depends on all earlier tokens, a change in the first few tokens invalidates everything after it. Moving the timestamp after the fixed instructions restores reuse. The tempting misconception is that the whole prompt must match, when only the shared leading portion needs to be identical.
options: The cache matches only identical leading tokens, so the changing timestamp at the start blocks any reuse
Prefix caching only applies when the entire prompt, user message included, matches a previous one exactly
The 3,000-token instruction block exceeds the size limit for a cached prefix, so it is evicted at once
Prefix caching only reuses context between turns of the same conversation, never across different users

bank.prompt: In a multi-turn chat, turn 10 carries about 6,000 tokens of earlier conversation plus a short new message. Predict how TTFT behaves across turns with and without the server reusing the conversation's cached context. Also say what happens if the cached entry is evicted.
bank.reference: Without reuse, every turn re-prefills the whole history, so TTFT keeps growing as the conversation gets longer. With reuse, only the new message's tokens need prefill, so TTFT stays small and fairly flat. If the cached entry is evicted, for example under memory pressure or after a long idle gap, that turn pays the full prefill cost again and TTFT spikes.

modules.title: Reasoning about real workloads
modules.objective: Apply prefill, decode and latency metrics to estimate and prioritize performance for chat, RAG, agent and batch workloads.

bank.prompt: A nightly job summarizes one million archived documents. Nobody reads the summaries until the next morning. Which metric should drive how you configure and evaluate this workload?
bank.reference: With no user waiting, what matters is finishing the whole job by the deadline at the lowest cost, which depends on aggregate throughput. Per-request metrics like TTFT or TPOT are interactive concerns, and optimizing them usually means smaller batches that lower throughput and raise cost.
options: Aggregate throughput and cost per million tokens for the whole job
p99 time to first token, since slow starts delay the whole job
Time per output token, since it sets how fast each summary streams
p50 end-to-end latency per request, kept as low as possible

bank.prompt: A chat endpoint shows a TTFT of 0.4 s and a TPOT of 25 ms. A typical reply is 400 output tokens. Roughly how long does a user wait until the full reply has finished streaming?
bank.reference: Total latency is roughly \( \text{TTFT} + (N_{out}-1)\cdot\text{TPOT} \approx 0.4 + 399 \times 0.025 \approx 10.4 \) s. Quoting only TTFT confuses when the reply starts with when it finishes, and multiplying output tokens by TTFT treats every token as paying the prefill cost.
options: About 10.4 seconds
About 0.4 seconds
About 160 seconds
About 1 second

bank.prompt: Your team changed a RAG feature to retrieve more chunks per query. The diagram shows dashboard latency before and after the deploy. Traffic volume did not change. What is the most likely explanation for the pattern?
bank.reference: TTFT rose sharply while TPOT barely moved, which points to prefill: more retrieved chunks means more input tokens to process before the first token. Longer answers would raise total latency but not TTFT, because output length is decided after the first token is produced.
options: Retrieved context made prompts much longer, so prefill per request takes longer
The model now writes longer answers, which pushes back the first token
Decode became memory-bandwidth bound after the change, slowing every token
Streaming chunk size grew, so the client waits longer to render tokens

bank.prompt: A customer-facing chat assistant and a nightly job that reclassifies 2 million support tickets share one model deployment. Explain how you would prioritize the two workloads and which kind of metric you would hold each one to.
bank.reference: Chat should get priority, with targets on per-request latency such as p95 or p99 TTFT and TPOT, which means keeping its batch sizes or concurrency low enough to meet them. The ticket job should run as lower-priority or preemptible work, ideally in large batches or off-peak, judged on throughput, cost and finishing before its deadline rather than per-request latency.

bank.prompt: You swap a chat model for a reasoning model. For the same prompt, the visible answer stays about 300 tokens, but the model now generates about 3,000 hidden reasoning tokens before answering. What should you expect?
bank.reference: Reasoning tokens are produced one at a time in decode like any other output, so the visible answer is delayed by roughly 3,000 times TPOT, and providers typically bill them as output tokens. Hidden does not mean free: the user does not see the tokens, but the model still generates every one of them.
options: The answer starts much later and costs more, since reasoning tokens are decoded and billed as output
Latency is unchanged, because hidden reasoning tokens are never streamed to the user
Only prompt processing time rises, because reasoning happens during the prefill phase
Cost rises but latency does not, because reasoning tokens are generated in parallel

bank.prompt: An agent completes a task by making 8 sequential LLM calls, appending tool results to the context after each one. Only the final answer is shown to the user. Which latency metric best reflects what the user experiences, and why is TTFT of a single call a poor guide here?
bank.reference: The user feels the end-to-end task time, which is the sum of every call's full latency (its TTFT plus its output tokens times TPOT) plus tool time, because each step must finish before the next starts. A single call's TTFT ignores the decode time of intermediate outputs nobody sees and the growing prefill cost as the context lengthens each step.

bank.prompt: A RAG request has 8,000 input tokens and 150 output tokens. Your deployment prefills at about 10,000 tokens per second and has a TPOT of 20 ms. Ignoring queueing, which phase dominates the request's total latency?
bank.reference: Prefill takes about \( 8000 / 10000 = 0.8 \) s, while decode takes about \( 150 \times 0.02 = 3 \) s. Prefill processes tokens in parallel and decode produces them one at a time, so far more input tokens does not imply prefill dominates.
options: Decode dominates: about 3 seconds versus under 1 second of prefill
Prefill dominates, since the input is about fifty times longer than the output
Prefill dominates: about 8 seconds versus 3 seconds of decode
They are roughly equal, since both phases process the same context

bank.prompt: You are building inline code autocomplete for an IDE. Each request sends about 1,500 tokens of surrounding code and returns about 15 tokens. The suggestion is shown only once it is complete, and the developer pauses waiting for it. Which metric deserves the tightest target?
bank.reference: The developer waits for the whole short suggestion, so the wait is queueing plus prefill of about 1,500 tokens plus about 15 decode steps. That full per-request end-to-end latency is the number to hold tight. Neither TTFT nor TPOT alone captures it: with typical numbers, 15 decode steps can take as long as prefill. Aggregate throughput metrics measure capacity, not what one waiting developer feels.
options: End-to-end latency per request, from keystroke until the full suggestion is ready
TPOT alone, because it sets how fast the suggestion streams token by token
Aggregate output tokens per second across the serving cluster
Aggregate decode throughput per GPU during peak hours

bank.prompt: The diagram shows the phases of a typical request on your summarization endpoint. You are asked to cut total latency as much as possible with one change. Which change helps most?
bank.reference: Decode takes about \( 600 \times 0.03 = 18 \) s, so halving output saves roughly 9 s, while queueing and prefill together are under 1 s. Optimizing prefill or queueing is tempting because they come first and feel like the delay, but the long tail of decode dominates total time.
options: Halve the output length with a more concise answer format
Halve the prompt length by trimming the system prompt
Remove queueing by adding capacity for this route
Enable prefix caching so most of prefill is skipped

bank.prompt: Product asks whether prompting the model to answer in about 200 tokens instead of about 800 will noticeably speed up a streaming chat feature. TTFT is small compared with total reply time. Predict the effect on total reply time and on TTFT, and explain why.
bank.reference: Total reply time should drop to roughly a quarter, because decode time scales about linearly with the number of output tokens and decode dominates here. TTFT stays about the same, since it depends on queueing and prefill of the input, which the change barely affects.

bank.prompt: After raising the maximum batch size on your chat deployment, the dashboard shows aggregate output tokens per second up 40 percent. The same week, users complain that replies feel sluggish. What is the most likely reading of the metrics?
bank.reference: Aggregate throughput sums tokens across all concurrent requests, so it can rise while each request's TPOT gets worse as more sequences share each decode step. Assuming higher throughput means lower latency is the classic misreading; the two trade off against each other.
options: Bigger batches raised total tokens per second but slowed each user's stream; check per-request TPOT
Throughput rose, so per-request latency must have fallen; the complaints likely come from network issues
Aggregate throughput counts prefill tokens, so the gain is illusory and nothing changed for users
The model is now producing shorter answers, which users perceive as lower quality rather than slow

bank.reference: Only the tail spikes in two fixed windows while the median is unaffected, which suggests some requests are waiting in a queue or behind heavy prefill work during those hours, most likely a scheduled or bursty workload such as a batch job with long prompts sharing the deployment. Check what runs at those times on the same hardware and the queue wait or prompt length distribution during the spikes.

bank.prompt: You must run 50,000 evaluation prompts through a hosted model, and results are needed by tomorrow morning. No one watches individual responses. Which approach fits the workload best?
bank.reference: Offline work is judged on finishing by the deadline at low cost, so large batches and discounted batch interfaces, which trade turnaround time for price, fit well. Optimizing per-request latency for work nobody is watching pays for speed that adds no value and usually lowers total throughput.
options: Use a batch interface or offline queue with large batches, optimizing cost and accepting slow individual responses
Stream every response and minimize TTFT so that the overall job finishes sooner
Send requests one at a time to keep per-request latency low and avoid any rate limits
Route the job to the lowest-TPOT premium tier so that each individual request finishes fastest

bank.prompt: Load tests on one deployment give TPOT of 20 ms at 8 concurrent requests, 28 ms at 16, 42 ms at 32 and 60 ms at 64, with throughput rising at each step. Chat has a TPOT target of 50 ms; a separate pool runs document tagging. How should you set concurrency?
bank.reference: Chat should use the highest concurrency that still meets its 50 ms TPOT target, which is around 32, while tagging has no per-token target and should run where throughput and cost are best. Maximizing throughput everywhere violates the interactive SLO, and minimizing latency everywhere wastes capacity on offline work.
options: Cap chat near 32 concurrent requests and run the tagging pool at 64
Run both at 64, since the higher throughput lowers cost for everyone
Run both at 8, since the lowest TPOT is always best for every user
Cap chat at 64 and tagging at 8, since tagging prompts tend to be longer

bank.prompt: A reasoning model on your deployment typically emits about 4,000 thinking tokens before its visible answer, at a TPOT of 25 ms. The thinking is hidden from the user. Roughly how long after the request does the visible answer begin?
bank.reference: Hidden thinking tokens are decoded at the normal rate, so they add about \( 4000 \times 0.025 = 100 \) s before the first visible token. Treating hidden tokens as free is the key mistake: from the user's point of view, the effective time to first useful token includes all of the reasoning.
options: About 100 seconds plus the TTFT
Roughly the TTFT alone, since thinking is hidden
About 10 seconds, since thinking decodes faster
About 4 seconds, at one millisecond per hidden token

bank.prompt: After switching an agent pipeline to a reasoning model, cost per task roughly tripled even though the prompts are unchanged and the visible answers are the same length. Explain the most likely cause and how you would confirm it from usage data.
bank.reference: The reasoning model generates many hidden reasoning tokens that providers typically bill as output tokens, and output tokens are usually priced higher than input, so cost rises even though visible answers did not change. Confirm it by checking the per-request usage breakdown for reasoning or total output token counts compared with the visible answer length.
